nameStory: The name 'stinkwort' tells you everything you need to know about this plant's most memorable feature! When you brush against its sticky leaves or crush them, they release a strong, camphor-like smell that's hard to forget. The 'wort' part is an old English word meaning plant or herb, so this is literally 'the stinky plant.'
description: Stinkwort is a bushy, branching plant that can grow quite tall - up to about 4 feet high. It's covered in narrow, pointed leaves that feel sticky to the touch and smell strongly of camphor when disturbed. The plant produces clusters of small yellow daisy-like flowers, and the whole thing has a somewhat weedy, unkempt appearance that helps it stand out from our native New England plants.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Touch a leaf and you'll immediately notice the sticky, resinous coating and strong camphor smell - like a cross between eucalyptus and mothballs. The leaves are long, narrow, and pointed at both ends with small teeth along the edges.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small yellow daisy-like flowers appear in clusters, each about half an inch across. Look closely and you'll see the typical sunflower family structure with yellow petals (ray florets) surrounding a central disc of tiny tube-shaped flowers.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a bushy, much-branched shrub-like plant that can reach your shoulder height or taller. The branching pattern gives it a somewhat scraggly, irregular outline.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Fluffy-tipped seeds with tiny barbs that stick to clothing and fur. The seeds feel slightly rough when rubbed between your fingers due to these microscopic hooks.

habitat: As a recent arrival to New England, stinkwort is most likely found in disturbed areas like roadsides, vacant lots, and waste ground. It prefers sunny spots with well-drained soil and tends to pop up in places where the natural plant community has been disrupted. Keep an eye out near parking areas, construction sites, and along transportation corridors where seeds might arrive on vehicles.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and begin their rapid growth, developing the characteristic sticky leaves. The camphor smell is already noticeable even on small plants.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering time when the yellow daisy-like blooms appear in abundance. This is when the plant is most conspicuous and easiest to identify from a distance.
seasonality.fall: Seeds develop their fluffy, barbed tips and begin dispersing. The plant may continue blooming into early fall in warmer areas.
seasonality.winter: As a subshrub, some woody stems may persist through winter, though the plant dies back significantly in New England's harsh climate.

funFact: This innocent-looking plant is so problematic for livestock that the barbs on its seeds can actually be fatal to grazing animals by damaging their digestive systems, and any animals that do manage to eat it will produce meat and milk that tastes terrible due to the plant's oils!
confusionNotes: With only 4 recorded sightings in New England, you're unlikely to confuse stinkwort with anything else simply because it's so rare here! If you think you've found it, the sticky, camphor-scented leaves are the dead giveaway - no native New England plant has quite this combination of stickiness and smell.
contextualKnowledge: Stinkwort is considered an invasive species that's native to southern Europe and western Asia. It's been causing major problems in places like California where it threatens wine production, so any sightings in New England should be reported to local environmental authorities as it represents a potential new invasion.
compareHints: Since stinkwort is the only member of its genus in our region, compare it to other yellow-flowered members of the sunflower family. Unlike our native goldenrods which have tiny flowers in dense clusters, stinkwort has distinct daisy-like flowers. Unlike native asters which bloom in fall, stinkwort lacks the strong camphor scent and sticky leaves that make this species unmistakable.
